title: What Is a Lesson Aim?
brief: Define a lesson aim as a statement of what learners will be able to do by the end of a lesson, distinguishing it clearly from a description of classroom activities. Draw on the module's language about teachers creating 'learning opportunities with clear guidelines and outcomes' and the idea that checklists are 'clearly linked to the learning objectives' to show that aims describe intended learning results, not procedures. Explain that an aim answers the question 'What will students have learned?' rather than 'What will students do?' Use the module's framing of the teacher as someone who 'creates learning opportunities with clear guidelines and outcomes, and then sets students in motion' to reinforce that the aim precedes and shapes every activity choice.

title: Outcome-Focused Language: 'Learners Will Be Able To…'
brief: Explain why lesson aims must be written in outcome-focused language centred on what learners will be able to do, rather than what the teacher will do or what activities will take place. Draw on the module's repeated references to 'learning objectives' and 'outcomes' — including the point that good checklists are 'clearly linked to the learning objectives' and that the teacher 'creates learning opportunities with clear guidelines and outcomes' — to show that outcomes must be made explicit and observable. Introduce the 'learners will be able to…' stem as the standard formulation, and explain how this phrasing keeps the focus on learner performance rather than teacher input or task completion.

title: Realistic Scope: Matching Aims to a Single Lesson
brief: Address the importance of writing aims that are realistic and achievable within the time and context of a single lesson. Use the module's discussion of lesson objectives — including the prompt asking observers to 'describe the lesson objectives' and consider 'how did the teacher evaluate whether the objectives were met during the lesson?' — to show that aims must be narrow enough to be assessed within the lesson itself. Draw also on the module's point that autonomous work 'may at first be unfamiliar to students who might need some time to learn it,' illustrating that teachers must account for learner readiness when scoping an aim. Explain that an aim covering too much ground cannot be meaningfully checked, while an aim that is too narrow may not justify a full lesson.

title: Aim vs. Activity: A Critical Distinction
brief: Clarify the difference between an aim (the intended learning outcome) and an activity (the task or procedure used to reach that outcome), using concrete examples drawn from the module. The module describes numerous classroom activities — vocabulary card games, mind maps, role-plays, peer feedback, and learning stations — none of which are aims in themselves; use these to illustrate that naming an activity ('students will do a mind map') is not the same as stating what students will learn from it. Reference the module's statement that 'the teacher creates learning opportunities with clear guidelines and outcomes' to reinforce that activities are vehicles for outcomes, not outcomes themselves. Show how the same activity (e.g., a peer feedback task) could serve different aims depending on what the teacher intends learners to be able to do afterwards.

title: Weak Aims vs. Strong Aims: Worked Examples
brief: Present a set of worked examples contrasting weak and strong lesson aims, drawing directly on activities and objectives mentioned in the module. For each weak aim, identify the specific problem — too vague, activity-focused, teacher-centred, or unrealistically broad — and rewrite it as a strong, outcome-focused aim using the 'learners will be able to…' formulation. Source material to draw on includes the vocabulary card game, the mind-map and sculpture task, the role-play and Q&A activity, and the storytelling lesson with comprehension questions; each provides a realistic classroom context from which a weak aim can be constructed and then improved. Ensure examples cover at least two common error types: aims that describe activities rather than outcomes, and aims that are too broad to assess in a single lesson.

title: Checking Your Aim: Can You Assess It?
brief: Explain how a well-written aim must be assessable — formally or informally — within the lesson, and show how teachers can use this as a self-check when writing aims. Draw on the module's repeated prompt to consider whether the teacher 'formally or informally assessed student performance or knowledge' and, if not, 'how could the teacher find out what the students learned during this lesson?' to establish assessment-readiness as a quality criterion for aims. Reference the module's point that checklists 'make expectations very clear' and help students 'accomplish and organize their work' as an example of how clear objectives enable both teaching and checking. Guide the reader to ask, after drafting an aim: 'How will I know at the end of the lesson whether this aim has been met?' — and to revise any aim that cannot be answered.
